**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Hardware expansion vs. utilisation improvement for our inference fleet

**Background**

We are approaching a decision point on our AI compute capacity. Our current fleet of eight GPUs is running at roughly 55% average utilisation, but that number hides significant variance: weekday business hours see sustained peaks above 90%, while nights and weekends sit near 15%. Queue times during peak periods have crept from seconds to minutes, and two product teams have told us they are delaying feature launches because they cannot get reliable access to the fleet. The default instinct — buy more hardware — deserves scrutiny, because the utilisation data suggests our real problem may be scheduling rather than supply.

**The case for buying more hardware**

The straightforward argument is that demand is growing and will keep growing. Our usage has roughly doubled over the past year, and if that trend holds, even perfect scheduling buys us only a few quarters of headroom. Additional capacity would also give us genuine reliability headroom: right now, a single hardware failure during peak hours degrades service for everyone, because we have no slack to absorb it. Latency-sensitive workloads — the interactive inference paths our customer-facing features depend on — are the first to suffer when the fleet saturates, and no amount of clever queueing fixes the physics of a full GPU.

There is also a hidden cost to congestion that doesn't show up on an invoice. Engineers waiting on jobs, teams shipping features late, and the opportunity cost of experiments nobody runs because the queue is too long — these are real, if hard to quantify. Buying capacity makes that constraint disappear immediately and lets the team focus on product work rather than capacity triage.

**The case for improving utilisation**

But the utilisation numbers tell a different story. Fifty-five percent average utilisation means we own nearly twice the hardware our average demand requires; we simply hold it in the wrong shape. Our largest jobs are long-running batch workloads that occupy GPUs continuously even when their actual compute intensity is bursty. Interactive and batch work share the same pool with no priority separation, so a nightly training run can block a customer-facing request. We have never implemented fractional GPU allocation, so a job needing 10% of a card takes a whole one. And we have no mechanism for shifting batch work into the overnight and weekend troughs, which represent enormous idle capacity we are already paying depreciation on.

The engineering work to fix this — a proper scheduler with workload classes, batch deferral windows, and finer-grained allocation — is perhaps six to eight weeks of effort from two engineers. Against that, the quote for four additional GPUs, including hosting, power, and networking, is a substantial recurring commitment that locks us into a capacity curve we may not need if demand patterns shift.

**Reversibility and risk**

This is where the asymmetry matters. Buying hardware is largely irreversible at our scale. Once we sign a hosting contract or take delivery of cards, that spend is committed whether or not we need it, and reselling specialised hardware recovers a fraction of its cost. Improving utilisation is the opposite: it is an investment in software and process that pays off regardless of what we later decide. If we fix scheduling and then still need more capacity, the scheduler work is not wasted — it makes the new hardware more effective too. If we buy hardware first and never fix scheduling, we will simply saturate the larger fleet the same way and be back here in a year, having paid twice.

**Recommendation**

Commit to the utilisation work first, with a hard decision gate. We should spend the next two months building workload separation, batch deferral, and fractional allocation, targeting 75% sustained utilisation with peak queue times under ten seconds. If we hit that target and demand continues to grow, we will have earned a much better-informed purchase decision — and possibly deferred it by two quarters. If we miss the target because the work proves harder than expected, we escalate the hardware request immediately with the benefit of knowing exactly what the scheduler could and could not deliver.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be honest about what we don't know. Our demand forecast is extrapolated from one year of growth in a product area that may not grow linearly. The 55% utilisation figure may understate real contention in ways our coarse metrics don't capture. And the engineering estimate carries normal risk of surprises. The two-month gate is designed precisely to convert that uncertainty into evidence before we commit capital. The cost of waiting, in engineer time and some continued peak-hour friction, is modest and recoverable. The cost of buying prematurely is not.

I recommend we approve the utilisation project now and schedule the capacity decision for the end of the quarter.
